implementation_notes: In Node.js the channel is an EventEmitter: on/addListener registers listener functions under an event name, emit calls them synchronously in registration order with the emitted arguments, and once/off/removeListener manage the lifecycle; extending EventEmitter or holding one as a field replaces the subscriber registry entirely. Listeners are plain functions, so closures and methods both work, and the same API backs streams, servers and process itself. The classic structure survives only as the decision of who owns the emitter and which event names are part of a module's contract.
pitfalls: emit is synchronous: a slow listener blocks the emitter, and an exception thrown by a listener propagates out of emit to the publisher.
Listeners are strong references; forgetting removeListener (or registering a fresh closure per request) is the classic EventEmitter memory leak.
Passing an unbounded number of listeners logs MaxListenersExceededWarning - fix the ownership, do not just raise the limit.

variants.name: WHATWG EventTarget and CustomEvent
variants.implementation_notes: Browsers, workers, Deno and Bun expose the EventTarget interface on any object that can receive events, including a plain new EventTarget(): addEventListener(type, handler, options) subscribes, dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent(type, { detail })) publishes, and removeEventListener or an AbortSignal unsubscribes. Dispatch semantics are the platform's - bubbling for DOM nodes, a single Event argument, cancellable events - and Node.js implements EventTarget as well, so the same bus code runs in both runtimes. Use it when the code already lives in a DOM or platform-event world; EventEmitter remains the Node-idiomatic choice for server-side modules.
pitfalls: An inline arrow passed to addEventListener cannot be removed afterwards: keep the function reference or pass an AbortSignal.
Events dispatched on DOM nodes bubble to ancestors, so an application bus should be a dedicated EventTarget rather than a document or element.
Browser dispatch is synchronous and listener exceptions are reported as uncaught errors without stopping the remaining listeners' registration order guarantees.
